# Designing a High-Performance Distributed ACID Property Graph Database

**Overview:** This report details the low-level engineering of a novel distributed property-graph database engine. We focus on the storage, indexing, concurrency, and coordination mechanisms (not the GQL query language) needed to achieve **ACID compliance** at scale. Key topics include on-disk data layout, mutable persistent structures, write-ahead logging (WAL) and recovery (ARIES), encryption at rest, graph-specific sharding strategies, and distributed protocols for consistency (Raft consensus, two-phase commit) and fault tolerance. Throughout, we ground design decisions in recent systems research (last 10–15 years) and include Zig code snippets and diagrams to illustrate critical components.

## Storage Engine and Binary Data Layout

**Disk Page Structure:** The database uses a paged storage model with slotted pages to store variable-length records (vertices, edges, index entries). A slotted page contains a **page header** and an array of **slots (pointers)** that reference the actual records. The records (cells) grow from the page end backward, and the slot array grows from the front forward, with a free space region in between[\[1\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=Slotted%20pages%20work%20by%20splitting,many%20big%20databases%2C%20like%20PostgreSQL). This design allows efficient in-page allocation and deletion without immediate record movement. **Figure 1** shows an illustration of a slotted page layout. The header keeps metadata (e.g. page ID, page type, free space offsets) and each slot stores the offset and size of a record[\[2\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=The%20header%20region%20stores%20metadata,compression%2C%20sibling%20page%20ids%2C%20etc)[\[3\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=typedef%20struct%20PageHeader%20,PageHeader). When inserting a record, we decrease the free-space end pointer and copy the record bytes; we then add a new slot entry pointing to that location, updating the free space boundary[\[4\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=header,free_start)[\[5\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=cell_pointer.cell_location%20%3D%20header,cell_location%2C%20cell%2C%20cell_size). Removal is handled by marking a slot as unused (and optionally compacting the page later)[\[6\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=Removing%20an%20item%20also%20becomes,referenced). This layout is used for both graph data and indexes, providing stable in-page references (slot indexes) that remain valid even if the free space is reorganized.

![](data:image/png;base64,)  
_Figure 1: Slotted page layout with header, slot pointers (ptr1, ptr2, ...) growing from the front, free space in the middle, and record cells (cell1, cell2, ...) stored contiguously from the end. This design allows in-place updates and frees without shifting other records_[_\[1\]_](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=Slotted%20pages%20work%20by%20splitting,many%20big%20databases%2C%20like%20PostgreSQL)_._

**Vertex and Edge Storage:** We model the property graph using fixed-length _node records_ and _edge records_, supplemented by variable-length _property records_. Each **vertex (node)** has a unique ID and is stored in a node record containing essential fields: label/type, pointers or offsets to its property list, and pointers to its first outgoing and incoming edge (if any). Each **edge** is stored in an edge record that includes its source and target vertex IDs, edge label/type, and pointer to its property list. To efficiently traverse relationships, edges are doubly-linked: an edge record contains a pointer to the next edge in the source vertex’s adjacency list and another pointer to the next edge in the target’s adjacency list. This way, all outgoing edges of a vertex form a linked list (using the “next-out” pointers), and all incoming edges form another list (“next-in”). Traversals can follow these links to iterate neighbors without global index lookups. The cost is an extra write when adding or removing an edge (to update these pointers), but it yields fast local traversals. (This approach is inspired by Neo4j’s fixed-size record design, which uses linked lists for adjacency[\[7\]](https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/understanding-data-on-disk/#:~:text=Properties%20are%20stored%20as%20a,Each%20node%20and%20relationship).)

**Properties and Indexing:** Each vertex or edge can have an arbitrary set of properties (key–value pairs). Rather than storing all properties inline, we use separate **property records** to handle dynamic attributes efficiently. A node or edge record holds either a _small inline property_ or a pointer to a chain of property records. Each property record can store one or more (keyID, value) pairs (with keyIDs referencing a schema dictionary) and a pointer to the next property record[\[7\]](https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/understanding-data-on-disk/#:~:text=Properties%20are%20stored%20as%20a,Each%20node%20and%20relationship). This is similar to the linked list of property records in Neo4j’s storage engine[\[7\]](https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/understanding-data-on-disk/#:~:text=Properties%20are%20stored%20as%20a,Each%20node%20and%20relationship), allowing properties to be added without moving the main node/edge record. To find vertices or edges by property value (for filtered queries), we maintain **secondary indexes**. A typical secondary index is a **B+ tree** keyed by \[property_key, property_value\] mapping to the corresponding entity IDs. B+trees are a proven choice for database indexes, providing logarithmic search, range query support, and efficient sequential access by key order[\[8\]](https://pganalyze.com/blog/postgresql-vs-sql-server-btree-index-deduplication#:~:text=Postgres%20vs.%20SQL%20Server%3A%20B,balanced%20for%20consistent%20read%20performance)[\[9\]](https://rcoh.me/posts/postgres-indexes-under-the-hood/#:~:text=Postgres%20Indexes%20Under%20the%20Hood,of%20binary%20search%20trees). Each index is stored in pages using the slotted layout (for variable-length keys). Leaf pages contain (key, list-of-IDs) entries. We use **prefix compression** on keys within B+tree pages to reduce storage and I/O, and large ID lists may overflow to separate pages. The B+tree operations (search, insert, split) are implemented with careful concurrency control (latches) and logged for recovery – see below on WAL.

&lt;details open&gt;&lt;summary&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Example: Zig struct for a slotted page and record insertion&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/summary&gt;

const PAGE_SIZE = 4096;  
const PageType = enum(u8) { Free=0, Data=1, Index=2 };  
<br/>const PageHeader = packed struct {  
id: u32, // page identifier  
pt: PageType, // page type (data or index)  
free_start: u16, // offset to start of free space region  
free_end: u16, // offset to end of free space region  
free_total: u16, // total free bytes in page  
slot_count: u16, // number of slots (including free/deleted slots)  
flags: u16 // status flags (e.g., dirty, needs compaction)  
};  
<br/>const Slot = packed struct {  
offset: u16,  
size: u16  
};  
<br/>// Initialize a fresh page (called when a new page is allocated)  
pub fn initPage(page: \[\]u8, id: u32, pt: PageType) void {  
// Safety: assume \`page\` is PAGE_SIZE bytes, zero-initialized  
var hdr = &reinterpret(PageHeader, page\[0..\])\[0\];  
hdr.id = id;  
hdr.pt = pt;  
hdr.free_start = @sizeOf(PageHeader);  
hdr.free_end = PAGE_SIZE - 1;  
hdr.free_total = PAGE_SIZE - @sizeOf(PageHeader);  
hdr.slot_count = 0;  
hdr.flags = 0;  
}  
<br/>// Insert a record into the slotted page. Returns slot index or error if no space.  
pub fn insertRecord(page: \[\]u8, record: \[\]const u8) ?u16 {  
const hdr_ptr = &reinterpret(PageHeader, page\[0..\])\[0\];  
const rec_size = record.len;  
const needed = rec_size + @sizeOf(Slot);  
if (needed > hdr_ptr.free_total) return null; // not enough space  
// Compute target offsets for new record and slot  
const rec_offset = hdr_ptr.free_end - @intCast(u16, rec_size) + 1;  
const slot_index = hdr_ptr.slot_count;  
const slot_offset = hdr_ptr.free_start;  
// Copy record bytes into the free space region  
std.mem.copy(u8, page\[rec_offset .. rec_offset + rec_size\], record);  
// Create a new slot pointing to the record  
var slot = Slot{ .offset = rec_offset, .size = @intCast(u16, rec_size) };  
std.mem.copy(u8, page\[slot_offset .. slot_offset + @sizeOf(Slot)\], @bytesOf(slot));  
// Update header  
hdr_ptr.free_start += @sizeOf(Slot);  
hdr_ptr.free_end = rec_offset - 1;  
hdr_ptr.free_total = hdr_ptr.free_end - hdr_ptr.free_start + 1;  
hdr_ptr.slot_count += 1;  
return slot_index;  
}

_Description:_ We define a PageHeader with offsets tracking free space. On initPage, we set up the initial free space spanning the whole page[\[3\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=typedef%20struct%20PageHeader%20,PageHeader)[\[10\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=void,free_start). insertRecord checks space, then computes where to place the new record at the end of free space, writes the record bytes, and adds a new Slot at free_start pointing to it[\[4\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=header,free_start)[\[5\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=cell_pointer.cell_location%20%3D%20header,cell_location%2C%20cell%2C%20cell_size). The header is updated to reflect the consumed free space and increased slot count. &lt;/details&gt;

**Disk File Organization:** The database uses multiple file types to segregate data for access efficiency and manage different lifecycles. For example, we maintain a **Node file** (storing fixed-size node records in pages), an **Edge file** (edge records), a **Property file** (variable-size property records, possibly in a heap file format), and separate files for each index. This separation resembles Neo4j’s storage format where different store files hold nodes, relationships, and properties[\[7\]](https://neo4j.com/developer/kb/understanding-data-on-disk/#:~:text=Properties%20are%20stored%20as%20a,Each%20node%20and%20relationship). Grouping similar records together optimizes sequential I/O and buffer caching (e.g., scanning all nodes vs. all edges). Each file is logically a collection of pages managed by a buffer pool in memory. **Buffer Manager:** The buffer pool caches frequently used pages in memory to minimize disk I/O. It uses an LRU replacement policy (or a variant) to evict pages when memory is full[\[11\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=tolerance%20as%20follows,the%20redo%20log%20for%20each)[\[12\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=The%20original%20in,is%20successful%20only%20after%20all). The buffer manager implements the usual _steal/no-force_ policy from database systems: it may **steal** dirty pages (write them to disk) before commit if needed (for example, to free space in cache), and it does **not force** pages to disk at commit time[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=Semantics%2C%20or%20ARIES%2C%20is%20a,2)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=actions%20of%20a%20database%20before,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts). This improves throughput by allowing batching and re-ordering of writes, at the cost of requiring WAL and recovery (explained later) for correctness.

**Memory Layout and Caching:** In addition to the buffer pool (page cache), we implement an object-level cache for hot graph elements. For example, a very high-degree vertex’s adjacency list, once loaded, might be kept as an in-memory structure (e.g., an array of neighbor IDs) to speed up traversals. We use an LRU or LFU strategy to manage these cached objects[\[11\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=tolerance%20as%20follows,the%20redo%20log%20for%20each). This is analogous to G-Tran’s approach of treating the in-memory store as a cache and evicting to disk on pressure[\[11\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=tolerance%20as%20follows,the%20redo%20log%20for%20each)[\[15\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=entity%20in%F0%9D%91%87%20,for%20recovering%20the%20latest%20values). All caches are kept transactionally consistent: cached data is updated or invalidated on writes, and never bypasses isolation rules (the transaction manager and WAL ensure that uncommitted changes are not visible to other transactions even if cached).

## Transaction Concurrency Control (Isolation & Atomicity)

Maintaining **Isolation** in a multi-user system requires a suitable **concurrency control protocol**. We consider common approaches — two-phase locking (2PL), optimistic CC (OCC), and multi-version CC (MVCC) — each widely used in databases[\[16\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=databases%20to%20implement%20different%20isolation,the%20same%20time%20by%20main%02taining). Given the graph workload characteristics (irregular access, potentially large read/write sets due to multi-hop traversals[\[17\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=traversal,critical%20issue%20for%20dis%02tributed%20graph)), we choose a **strict two-phase locking** as the default for its robustness and simplicity[\[16\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=databases%20to%20implement%20different%20isolation,the%20same%20time%20by%20main%02taining)[\[18\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=version%20concurrency%20control%20%28MVCC%29%20,incurs%20a%20higher%20storage%20overhead). In strict 2PL, a transaction must hold all its exclusive locks until commit, preventing dirty writes and reads. This ensures **serializability** (the strictest isolation)[\[19\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=both%20serializability%20,2PL%20is%20the%20most%20common). Every vertex and edge record is locked (using a fine-grained lock manager) before update; for read operations, we use shared locks. We avoid deadlocks by implementing a wait-die or wound-wait policy, or by deadlock detection with a waits-for graph (on detecting a cycle, a victim transaction is aborted). **Lock granularity:** The default is record-level locking, which is appropriate given that graph transactions tend to touch a specific subset of vertices/edges. Higher-level locks (e.g., on entire subgraphs or index ranges) can be introduced for bulk operations but are avoided in OLTP to maximize concurrency.

_Rationale:_ We opted for 2PL over OCC/MVCC after considering graph-specific patterns. OCC (which does all writes tentatively and validates at commit) can suffer high abort rates for long graph traversals that touch many nodes (higher probability of concurrent conflicts)[\[17\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=traversal,critical%20issue%20for%20dis%02tributed%20graph)[\[20\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=read%2Fwrite%20sets,69%5D.%20Tradi%02tional). MVCC (maintaining multiple versions with timestamps) offers readers a consistent snapshot without locking[\[16\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=databases%20to%20implement%20different%20isolation,the%20same%20time%20by%20main%02taining), which is great for read-heavy workloads, but it imposes extra storage overhead for versions[\[21\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=transactions%20in%20three%20steps%3A%20process%2C,incurs%20a%20higher%20storage%20overhead) and complexity in garbage collection. In a graph OLTP scenario (with frequent writes, e.g., adding relationships, updating properties), MVCC’s benefits might not justify its cost. However, our design could be extended to support **snapshot isolation** (SI) for long-running analytical reads by keeping old versions – in fact, G-Tran demonstrates supporting both serializability and SI in a graph DB[\[22\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=Concurrency%20Control%20Protocols,phase%20locking)[\[23\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=both%20serializability%20,2PL%20is%20the%20most%20common) by toggling CC mechanisms. To keep our core design straightforward, we use strict 2PL (which yields serializable isolation by default). This choice aligns with many transactional graph systems (e.g., Titan/JanusGraph when backed by a transactional store, or Neo4j’s lock manager for ACID operations).

**Index Concurrency:** Indexes (B+ trees) use latch-based concurrency (lightweight mutexes) for thread-safe access to their pages. We implement **lock-coupling (crabbing)**: as a transaction traverses the B+tree, it acquires latches on nodes (shared for read, exclusive for modifications) and holds them until it moves to the next node, then releases the previous latch. This prevents inconsistencies during splits and merges. For updates, we also ensure a transaction acquires an appropriate data lock on the indexed item (to synchronize with operations on the base graph data). These index operations are integrated into the overall transaction so that they commit or abort together with graph changes. All modifications (node splits, etc.) are logged in the WAL with _physiological_ log records[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=To%20gather%20the%20necessary%20information,TT)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=Redo%2C%20Undo%2C%20Previous%20Sequence%20Number%29,taken%20within%20the%20specific%20transaction) (i.e., log records contain enough info to redo/undo changes at the page level, identified by page ID and slot).

**Atomicity and Consistency:** Atomicity (“all or nothing” execution of transactions) and consistency (transactions take the database from one valid state to another) are ensured by the interplay of the above mechanisms with the WAL and recovery (next section). By using strict 2PL and WAL, we guarantee that any transaction that commits has fully applied all its updates to the database, and if it aborts (or the system crashes before commit), none of its partial changes persist. The database enforces any integrity constraints (unique indexes, etc.) at commit time to uphold consistency – for example, a constraint check (like no duplicate node ID or edge) can be done as part of the transaction’s final phase under locks.

## Write-Ahead Logging and Recovery (Durability)

To provide **Durability** and crash recovery, the system employs a **write-ahead log (WAL)** following the ARIES algorithm (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=In%20computer%20science%20%2C%20Algorithms,2)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=Three%20main%20principles%20lie%20behind,ARIES)). Write-ahead logging means **any change to the database is first recorded in the log on stable storage, and the log is flushed to disk before the actual data pages are written**[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=Three%20main%20principles%20lie%20behind,ARIES). Our WAL records are appended to a sequential log file (or set of files) stored on disk (often on a separate device for performance). Each log record minimally contains: the transaction ID, the affected page or object ID, the before-image (undo information) and after-image (redo information) of the change, and pointers linking related log records (previous log LSN for that transaction)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=The%20dirty%20page%20table%20keeps,last%20log%20entry%20they%20created)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=Every%20transaction%20implicitly%20begins%20with,entry%20for%20the%20transaction). We include special **commit** log records when a transaction successfully completes, and **abort** records if it is rolled back. Using WAL with flush-on-commit ensures that once we acknowledge a commit, the transaction’s effects will survive any crash (durability).

**ARIES Recovery Procedure:** In case of a crash or restart, we perform the ARIES recovery in three passes[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=The%20recovery%20works%20in%20three,database%20in%20a%20consistent%20state):

- **Analysis Pass:** Read the log forward from the last checkpoint to identify which transactions were active (in-flight) at the time of crash and which pages were dirty. We reconstruct the **Transaction Table** (active txns and their last log LSN) and **Dirty Page Table** (pages with in-memory changes not on disk, and the LSN of the first update to each)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=To%20gather%20the%20necessary%20information,TT)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=The%20dirty%20page%20table%20keeps,last%20log%20entry%20they%20created). This tells us where to start redo.
- **Redo Pass:** We “repeat history” by replaying log records from the oldest dirty page LSN onwards[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=%2A%20Write,repeated%20in%20the%20event%20of). We redo every idempotent update from the log to bring the database back to the exact state it was in at crash time[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=the%20object%20are%20written%20to,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts). This includes re-applying uncommitted updates of transactions that hadn’t committed yet (they will be undone in the next phase). By repeating history, we restore the pages to their pre-crash contents, including any locked or interim states, which simplifies the logic (as ARIES argues[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=the%20object%20are%20written%20to,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts)).
- **Undo Pass:** For any transactions that were active (did not commit) at crash time, we proceed to undo their changes, working backward from the end of the log (the last LSN of each loser transaction)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=actions%20of%20a%20database%20before,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts). As we undo an operation, we generate a **compensation log record (CLR)** to log the undo action[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=During%20a%20recovery%2C%20or%20while,because%20CLR%20is%20never%20reverted). CLRs ensure that if a crash happens during recovery, we won’t repeat the same undo after restart (the CLR notes that a certain original update was undone)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=special%20kind%20of%20log%20record,because%20CLR%20is%20never%20reverted). We continue until all aborted transactions’ effects are removed, leaving the database in a consistent state containing only committed transactions.

**Checkpointing:** To avoid an ever-growing log and speed up recovery, we use fuzzy checkpoints. A checkpoint periodically records the current state (transaction table and dirty page table) to the log, so that on crash we can begin analysis from the last checkpoint rather than the log start. Our checkpoints are _fuzzy_ (the system isn’t quiesced; transactions can be ongoing). We write a begin-checkpoint record, gather the tables, then write an end-checkpoint record with the lists. This is logged with the LSN, and we also persist a pointer to it (in a master record on disk). During recovery, we start at the last checkpoint LSN, reconstruct the state, then scan forward[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=In%20computer%20science%20%2C%20Algorithms,2)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=actions%20of%20a%20database%20before,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts).

&lt;details open&gt;&lt;summary&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Example: Zig pseudo-code for writing WAL records&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/summary&gt;

const WAL = struct {  
fd: std.fs.File,  
// Write a log record to WAL (returns LSN = log sequence number)  
pub fn appendRecord(self: \*WAL, buf: \[\]const u8) !u64 {  
// Atomically write the bytes to the log file (at end)  
try self.fd.writeAll(buf);  
// In a real system, we would maintain an in-memory LSN counter or use file position.  
// Here we assume file.tell() gives us the LSN after write.  
const lsn = try self.fd.tell();  
return lsn;  
}  
};  
<br/>// Example structure of a log record (simplified, variable-length):  
const LogRecordType = enum(u8) { Update, Commit, Abort };  
<br/>const LogRecordHeader = packed struct {  
recType: LogRecordType,  
txID: u32,  
prevLSN: u64, // LSN of previous log record for this tx  
undoNextLSN: u64, // for CLRs: LSN to undo next (points to earlier update to undo)  
pageID: u32,  
payloadSize: u16 // length of redo/undo data following header  
};  
<br/>// Pseudo-code: logging an update (with before and after image diff)  
fn logUpdate(wal: \*WAL, tx: \*Transaction, pageID: u32, before: \[\]const u8, after: \[\]const u8) !void {  
var hdr = LogRecordHeader{  
.recType = .Update,  
.txID = tx.id,  
.prevLSN = tx.lastLSN,  
.undoNextLSN = 0, // not a CLR  
.pageID = pageID,  
.payloadSize = @intCast(u16, before.len + after.len)  
};  
var recordBuffer: \[256\]u8 = undefined;  
const headerBytes = @bytesOf(hdr);  
// Assemble the log record bytes (header + before-image + after-image)  
var off: u16 = 0;  
std.mem.copy(u8, recordBuffer\[off .. off+headerBytes.len\], headerBytes);  
off += @intCast(u16, headerBytes.len);  
std.mem.copy(u8, recordBuffer\[off .. off+before.len\], before);  
off += @intCast(u16, before.len);  
std.mem.copy(u8, recordBuffer\[off .. off+after.len\], after);  
off += @intCast(u16, after.len);  
const recBytes = recordBuffer\[0..off\];  
const lsn = try wal.appendRecord(recBytes);  
tx.lastLSN = lsn;  
// Mark page as dirty in Dirty Page Table etc. (not shown)  
}

_Description:_ We define a simple WAL struct with an appendRecord method to write log bytes (in practice, this would also flush or group-commit them to disk). Each log record has a header with fields similar to ARIES (transaction ID, type, prevLSN for linking records, etc.)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=The%20dirty%20page%20table%20keeps,last%20log%20entry%20they%20created)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=Every%20transaction%20implicitly%20begins%20with,entry%20for%20the%20transaction). The logUpdate function builds an update record containing a before-image and after-image of the modified data and writes it. This is a simplified illustration – real systems might log physical redo and logical undo information and use checksums, etc. &lt;/details&gt;

Our WAL ensures **Steal/No-Force safety:** Because we allow dirty pages to be flushed before commit (steal) and don’t force flush pages on commit (no-force), WAL is essential. The WAL _redo_ info lets us reapply updates that were on the log but might not have made it to disk, and _undo_ info lets us roll back changes that made it to disk from uncommitted transactions[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=In%20computer%20science%20%2C%20Algorithms,2)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=the%20object%20are%20written%20to,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts). By tagging each page with a **pageLSN** (the LSN of the latest update applied to that page), we can optimize redo: we only redo an update if its LSN is greater than the page’s disk LSN, indicating the page on disk is out-of-date relative to the log. This follows ARIES’s _repeating history_ approach[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=the%20object%20are%20written%20to,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts). During normal operation, we also write **flush markers** in the log (or use group commit) to know up to what LSN is safely on disk. We consider using an **I/O batching** or even an RDMA-friendly log if operating in a high-throughput environment, as recent research shows minimizing log write latency is crucial for scalability[\[39\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=we%20only%20discuss%20the%20design,processing%20by%20leveraging%20RDMA%202546)[\[40\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=transaction%20processing%20is%20the%20large,processing%20by%20leveraging%20RDMA%202546) (especially with distributed commits).

**Recovery Testing:** We regularly simulate crashes to test recovery logic (pulling the plug on nodes, etc.). The ARIES algorithm has been battle-tested in many systems[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=In%20computer%20science%20%2C%20Algorithms,2)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=no,2) (DB2, SQL Server, etc.), and we adhere to its principles. In particular, we log even the compensation records during undo[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=actions%20of%20a%20database%20before,the%20event%20of%20repeated%20restarts), ensuring **idempotence** of recovery (if a crash occurs mid-recovery, the next restart will see the CLRs and know those steps were undone already). This guarantees **atomicity**: transactions are all-or-nothing, even across failures[\[42\]](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/courses/cs262a-F12/lectures/lec05-aries-rev.pdf#:~:text=crash%21%20%EF%81%B6%20Desired%20Behavior%20after,T1T2T3T4T5)[\[43\]](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/courses/cs262a-F12/lectures/lec05-aries-rev.pdf#:~:text=Intended%20Functionality%E2%80%A2%20At%20any%20time%2C,by%20a%20transaction%20that%20committed).

## Security: Encryption at Rest and Trusted Execution

For sensitive applications, the engine supports **encryption-at-rest** to protect data files and WAL logs on disk. We implement **Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)**: all pages written to disk are encrypted using a strong cipher (e.g. AES-256 in XTS mode). A **master key** (stored in a secure wallet or Hardware Security Module HSM) is used to derive data encryption keys. The encryption/decryption is done in the buffer manager – when a page is read from disk, it is decrypted in memory (with keys in process memory or preferably in secure enclaves), and when written to disk it is encrypted[\[44\]](https://graphdb.ontotext.com/documentation/11.0/encryption.html#:~:text=Encryption%20%E2%80%94%20GraphDB%2011,encryption%2C%20encrypt%20repository%20data%2C). This ensures that data on disk or backups cannot be read if stolen. We also encrypt the write-ahead log, since it contains sensitive before/after images.

For higher security, the system can integrate with hardware **Trusted Execution Environments (TEE)** such as Intel SGX. In a TEE deployment, decryption of data and even query processing can occur inside an enclave so that the plaintext data is not exposed to the host OS or a rogue DBA[\[45\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=database%20administrator%20is%20malicious%2C%20when,The%20protocol%20supports)[\[46\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=trust%20in%20online%20services,8). Systems like EnclaveDB have demonstrated that running the storage engine and transaction manager inside SGX can ensure confidentiality and integrity even if the OS is compromised[\[47\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=the%20database%20runs%20in%20an,appends%20and%20truncation%2C%20and%20requires)[\[48\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=as%20password%20checkers%2C%20key%20management,enclaves%20and%20offer%20strong%20security). We follow a similar model for optional deployment: the enclave holds the keys and performs operations on sensitive data. The overhead (around 30-40% in EnclaveDB’s evaluation[\[49\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=concurrent%2C%20asynchronous%20appends%20and%20truncation%2C,memory%20database%20engine)) is considered acceptable for the added security in many cases. For example, the log integrity can be protected by a secure checksum or incremental MAC stored in enclave memory so that if an attacker tampers with the WAL on disk, the discrepancy is detected on recovery[\[50\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=which%20includes%20an%20in,C%29%20compared%20to).

**Key Management:** The system uses a two-tier key architecture. A short-lived **database key** encrypts pages; this key is stored in memory (and in the enclave if using SGX) and never written to disk. It is itself encrypted with a **master key** that is stored in an HSM or provided via a cloud key management service (e.g., AWS KMS) at startup[\[51\]](https://neo4j.com/news/neo4j-thales-graph-data-at-rest-encryption/#:~:text=Neo4j%2C%20the%20leader%20in%20graph,Thales%20Vormetric%20Transparent%20Encryption)[\[52\]](https://security.stackexchange.com/questions/279587/hsm-for-secure-encrypted-data-storage#:~:text=HSM%20for%20Secure%20Encrypted%20Data,anything%20else%20to%20decrypt). This way, compromising a database file yields only encrypted bytes, and the master key can be rotated or secured externally. We also support **cluster-wide key rotation**: new data is written with a new key while old pages gradually get re-encrypted in background (lazy re-encryption).

**Client-Server Encryption:** Though out of scope for on-disk, we mention that client connections use TLS for data in transit, and optional end-to-end encryption of query results using client-held keys is possible for highly sensitive fields (in which case the engine might operate on ciphertext or only in enclaves).

In summary, our engine ensures data at rest is encrypted and can leverage modern secure hardware to meet confidentiality requirements of mission-critical deployments. These measures have become standard as even graph databases (e.g., Neo4j Enterprise with customer-managed keys[\[53\]](https://neo4j.com/news/neo4j-thales-graph-data-at-rest-encryption/#:~:text=Neo4j%20%26%20Thales%20Team%20Up,Thales%20Vormetric%20Transparent%20Encryption) or AWS Neptune[\[52\]](https://security.stackexchange.com/questions/279587/hsm-for-secure-encrypted-data-storage#:~:text=HSM%20for%20Secure%20Encrypted%20Data,anything%20else%20to%20decrypt)) now offer at-rest encryption.

## Distributed Sharding and Graph Partitioning

To scale out, the database is deployed as a **cluster** of nodes, partitioning the graph across machines. A careful **sharding (partitioning) strategy** is critical, as graph data is highly interconnected and naïve partitioning can lead to excessive cross-node communication[\[54\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=database,connectedness%20of%20graph%20data%20may)[\[55\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=,and%20lower%20throughput%20in%20trans%02action). We support two primary partitioning models:

- **Edge-Cut Partitioning (vertex-centric):** Each vertex (and its incident edges) is assigned to a single partition. If an edge connects two vertices on different partitions, that edge is a _cut edge_ and will require network communication when traversed[\[56\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=In%20assigning%20vertices%20to%20partitions,of%20frequently%20traversed%20edges%20in). The goal is to minimize such cut edges by co-locating strongly related vertices[\[57\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=In%20assigning%20vertices%20to%20partitions,edges%20in%20the%20same%20partition). By default, we hash vertices by their ID to assign partitions (a **hash partitioning**: partition_id = vertex_id mod N), which yields a roughly even distribution[\[58\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=a%20distributed%20key%2Fvalue%20store,storage%20hosts%20and%20query%20hosts)[\[59\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=key%2Fvalue%20operations,storage%20hosts%20and%20query%20hosts). This random distribution offers balance and requires no upfront knowledge (JanusGraph’s default is similar, using random partition IDs for vertices[\[60\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=graph%20in%20an%20adjacency%20list,explicit%20partitioning%20is%20not%20supported)[\[61\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=There%20are%20two%20aspects%20to,edge%20cuts%20and%20vertex%20cuts)). However, a purely random edge-cut can place adjacent vertices apart, causing many traversals to go remote[\[62\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=between%20the%20vertices%20is%20called,edges%20in%20the%20same%20partition). We allow custom **ID placement strategies** for edge-cut: for example, assigning certain subgraphs or communities to the same partition (if the user/application can provide hints)[\[63\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Vertices%20are%20placed%20in%20a,optimizing%20the%20loading%20strategy%20to)[\[64\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=However%2C%20the%20strategy%20is%20limited%2C,option). In fact, JanusGraph allows a user-defined IDPlacementStrategy to control vertex-to-partition mapping[\[64\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=However%2C%20the%20strategy%20is%20limited%2C,option). In our engine, one could implement a strategy that groups vertices by some property (like tenants or graph communities) so that intra-group edges are local. Edge-cut is intuitive and keeps each vertex’s data localized, but it can suffer from **hotspots**: a high-degree vertex (with thousands of edges) all on one machine can overload that machine for hub-centric queries.
- **Vertex-Cut Partitioning (edge-centric):** This approach distributes edges among partitions, allowing a single high-degree vertex’s edges to be split across multiple servers[\[65\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=While%20edge%20cut%20optimization%20aims,issue%20on%20very%20large%20graphs)[\[66\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Cutting%20a%20vertex%20means%20storing,and%20removing%20the%20hot%20spot). In a vertex-cut, _edges_ are the unit of placement, and if a vertex has edges in multiple partitions, the vertex itself is replicated (or at least its ID and some info) on those partitions[\[67\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235950091_SBV-Cut_Vertex-Cut_Based_Graph_Partitioning_Using_Structural_Balance_Vertices#:~:text=Vertex,the%20resulting%20data%20partitions%3B)[\[68\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235950091_SBV-Cut_Vertex-Cut_Based_Graph_Partitioning_Using_Structural_Balance_Vertices#:~:text=Vertices%20www.researchgate.net%20%20While%20edge,the%20resulting%20data%20partitions%3B). The classic example is PowerGraph’s strategy for power-law graphs: high-degree vertices are cut into many pieces so that no single machine owns all its edges[\[65\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=While%20edge%20cut%20optimization%20aims,issue%20on%20very%20large%20graphs)[\[66\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Cutting%20a%20vertex%20means%20storing,and%20removing%20the%20hot%20spot). **Vertex cuts effectively distribute the load of hot vertices** by partitioning their adjacency list across the cluster[\[69\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=cuts%20are%20needed%20to%20address,issue%20on%20very%20large%20graphs)[\[66\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Cutting%20a%20vertex%20means%20storing,and%20removing%20the%20hot%20spot). Our design supports vertex-cut for specific labels or vertex groups marked as _partitioned_ (following JanusGraph’s approach of partitioning by vertex label[\[70\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=JanusGraph%20cuts%20vertices%20by%20label,in%20the%20manner%20described%20above)). For instance, one could mark a “Product” vertex (in an e-commerce graph) as partitioned, meaning all product vertices will have their edges split among all partitions, avoiding any single product node becoming a bottleneck[\[71\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=mgmt). The downside is the complexity: each partition holds a partial view of that vertex’s edges, so a traversal that needs all of them must gather from all partitions. Moreover, updates to vertex properties or global constraints require coordinating the replicated vertex across partitions. JanusGraph notes that their vertex-cut (they call it “vertex label partitioning”) has high overhead and is not generally recommended[\[72\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Warning). Thus, we expose vertex-cut as an _optional_ feature for extreme cases, while edge-cut (each vertex single-home) is the default.

**Choosing a Strategy – Hybrid:** In practice, a hybrid approach can work: use edge-cut for most vertices (for simplicity and locality), and selectively use vertex-cut for a small set of high-degree vertices (to alleviate hotspots)[\[73\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=In%20the%20example%20above%2C%20,also%20partitioned%2C%20causing%20unnecessary%20overhead)[\[74\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=there%20are%20thousands%20of%20products,have%20high%20degree%20are%20also). Our engine could, for example, automatically detect vertices whose degree exceeds a threshold and then partition their edges among shards (this would involve dynamically creating “ghost” vertices on other partitions to hold some edges). There is active research on optimal graph partitioning (which is NP-hard in general) – heuristics like METIS partitions, label propagation, or even machine-learning based partitioners could be integrated off-line to improve the partition quality[\[75\]](https://www.mathsci.ai/publication/Parallel-Computing-2000.pdf#:~:text=MathSci,The%20same%20approach)[\[76\]](https://ipads.se.sjtu.edu.cn/_media/publications/powerlyra-eurosys15.pdf#:~:text=edge,of%20PowerGraph%20for%2048%20partitions). For online operation, we favor simpler schemes (hash or range by vertex ID) for predictable performance and low overhead.

**Shard Identifiers and Mapping:** We identify partitions by integer IDs. The mapping from a vertex ID to a partition can be done via a modulus as mentioned, or by encoding the partition ID into bits of the vertex ID (as Systems like JanusGraph/Titan and IBM’s System G do[\[77\]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.03057#:~:text=First%20a%20vertex%20is%20uniquely,VID%20variable%20and%20the%20overall)[\[78\]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.03057#:~:text=adding%20a%20ver%02tex%20to%20a,VID%20variable%20and%20the%20overall)). For example, we can designate the high bits of a 64-bit vertex ID for the shard number and lower bits for local ID. That allows quickly determining the home partition of a vertex by inspecting its ID bits[\[77\]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.03057#:~:text=First%20a%20vertex%20is%20uniquely,VID%20variable%20and%20the%20overall)[\[79\]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.03057#:~:text=,the%20id%20that%20represents%20shards). Our Zig code below shows an example of composing such an ID.

&lt;details open&gt;&lt;summary&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Example: Zig function for vertex ID partition mapping&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/summary&gt;

const SHARD_BITS: u32 = 10; // allow up to 1024 shards  
const LABEL_BITS: u32 = 6; // up to 64 labels (types)  
const LOCAL_BITS: u32 = 48; // remaining for local ID (gives ~2.8e14 IDs per shard)  
<br/>fn makeVertexId(label: u8, shard: u16, local: u64) u64 {  
assert(label < (1 << LABEL_BITS));  
assert(shard < (1 << SHARD_BITS));  
assert(local < (1 << LOCAL_BITS));  
var id: u64 = 0;  
id |= (@intCast(u64, label) & ((1 << LABEL_BITS) - 1)) << (SHARD_BITS + LOCAL_BITS);  
id |= (@intCast(u64, shard) & ((1 << SHARD_BITS) - 1)) << LOCAL_BITS;  
id |= local & ((@as(u64, 1) << LOCAL_BITS) - 1);  
return id;  
}  
<br/>fn decodeVertexId(id: u64) struct { label: u8, shard: u16, local: u64 } {  
const label = @intCast(u8, id >> (SHARD_BITS + LOCAL_BITS));  
const shard = @intCast(u16, id >> LOCAL_BITS) & @intCast(u16, ((1 << SHARD_BITS) - 1));  
const local = id & ((@as(u64, 1) << LOCAL_BITS) - 1);  
return .{ .label = label, .shard = shard, .local = local };  
}

_Description:_ We pack a 64-bit vertex ID with fields for label, shard, and local counter. For example, 10 bits for shard yields up to 1024 shards. This aligns with System G’s description, where an internal vertex id = {LabelId, ShardId, LocalId}[\[77\]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.03057#:~:text=First%20a%20vertex%20is%20uniquely,VID%20variable%20and%20the%20overall)[\[79\]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.03057#:~:text=,the%20id%20that%20represents%20shards). Using this scheme, given an ID we can instantly get its home shard (for routing requests), and ensure global ID uniqueness. The label portion helps keep type information quickly accessible too. &lt;/details&gt;

**Dynamic Load Balancing:** As the data grows or access patterns change, we need to **balance load** across shards. We monitor metrics like number of vertices/edges per shard and the rate of queries or updates handled. If one shard becomes overloaded (storage or CPU hot), we can **split** it or **migrate** part of its data to another node. One approach is to use consistent hashing or virtual shards: e.g., if initial max_shards = 16, we actually allow 16 virtual slots – if a particular slot is too heavy, we split it into two and reassign half the vertex ID range to a new physical shard (this requires updating the mapping in a meta-service). Another approach is similar to Spanner’s directory-based partitioning[\[80\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=directory%20abstraction%2C%20which%20is%20used,development%2Fproduction%20uni%02verse%2C%20and%20a%20production)[\[81\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=Spanner%20is%20organized%20as%20a,unit%20of%20physical%20isolation%3A%20there), where the unit of movement is a group of contiguous keys; in a graph, this could be a range of vertex IDs or a subgraph identified by some key prefix. Our system includes a **metadata service** (see Coordination section) that can trigger re-partitioning: it would quiesce the affected partition (or do a live migration with careful locking), then copy data to the target and update partition maps. All such re-sharding operations are transactionally logged to ensure consistency (possibly using a meta-transaction via Raft to coordinate the change).

In summary, our sharding strategy is flexible: by default, hash-based edge-cuts for simplicity[\[58\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=a%20distributed%20key%2Fvalue%20store,storage%20hosts%20and%20query%20hosts), with the option to handle hotspot vertices via vertex-cuts[\[66\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Cutting%20a%20vertex%20means%20storing,and%20removing%20the%20hot%20spot). This hybrid approach, combined with online monitoring and rebalancing, ensures the distributed graph can scale while maintaining ACID guarantees (the next sections cover how distributed consistency is achieved).

## Distributed Replication and Fault Tolerance

**High Availability** is achieved by replicating each partition’s data across multiple nodes. We employ a **shared-nothing, quorum-based replication** mechanism. Specifically, each partition is managed as a **Raft consensus group** of R replicas (e.g., 3 or 5) across different machines. Raft is a leader-based consensus algorithm that ensures a replicated log of operations is kept consistent across nodes[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20achieves%20consensus%20via%20an,4)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20implements%20consensus%20by%20a,servers%20elect%20a%20new%20leader). One replica is the **Leader** for the partition and serves read/write requests; the others are **Followers** that replicate the leader’s log and apply updates. Raft guarantees that if a majority of replicas (⌈R/2⌉) have persisted a log entry and the leader has committed it, that entry is durable and will be seen by any future leaders[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Once%20the%20leader%20receives%20confirmation,of%20Log%20Matching%20is%20respected)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=the%20entry%20has%20been%20replicated%2C,of%20Log%20Matching%20is%20respected). This provides strong consistency (linearizability) for operations on that partition.

**Raft Protocol:** In our design, each partition’s update operations (transactions) are submitted to the Raft leader as log entries. The leader appends the entry to its local log and then sends **AppendEntries** RPCs to followers with the new log entries[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=The%20leader%20is%20responsible%20for,by%20all%20of%20the%20followers)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Once%20the%20leader%20receives%20confirmation,of%20Log%20Matching%20is%20respected). Once a majority of followers acknowledge the entry, it is considered **committed**, and the leader applies it to the storage engine state machine and responds to the client[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Once%20the%20leader%20receives%20confirmation,of%20Log%20Matching%20is%20respected)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=the%20entry%20has%20been%20replicated%2C,of%20Log%20Matching%20is%20respected). If the leader crashes, Raft’s **leader election** takes place: a follower with up-to-date log will time out and become a candidate, soliciting votes from others; if it wins a majority, it becomes the new leader and continues operation[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20achieves%20consensus%20via%20an,4)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20implements%20consensus%20by%20a,servers%20elect%20a%20new%20leader). Raft ensures at most one leader at a time and that new leaders have all committed entries from previous terms, preserving consistency[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20is%20a%20consensus%20,Tolerant.%5B%203)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20is%20not%20a%20Byzantine,1). Our engine uses Raft rather than Paxos for understandability and ease of implementation[\[92\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=The%20Storage%20Service%20is%20designed,as%20the%20physical%20data%20storage)[\[93\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=A%20quorum%20consensus%20protocol%20,storage%20hosts%20and%20query%20hosts) – this matches industry practice, as Raft’s clarity has led to many production systems using it (etcd, CockroachDB, Neo4j’s causal clusters, etc.).

**Replication of WAL vs. Commands:** Instead of replicating low-level WAL bytes, we replicate logical operations or whole transactions in the Raft log. Practically, the leader can group the writes of a transaction into a Raft log entry (or series of entries), and followers apply them under the same serial order. We ensure that the commit of a transaction isn’t acknowledged until the Raft log containing it is durably replicated on a majority. This way, even if the leader fails immediately after acking, the new leader will still have those committed transactions in its log. The storage engine on each replica uses the WAL mainly for local recovery (e.g., if a single node crashes and comes back, it can recover), but cluster-wide durability is governed by the replicated log (Raft). A nice property of using Raft here is we avoid the classic 2PC durability problem: if a leader fails after committing but before followers got the data, Raft won’t consider it committed unless a majority had it, thereby **mitigating availability issues of two-phase commit by running it over Paxos/Raft**[\[94\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=have%20claimed%20that%20general%20two,Paxos%20mitigates%20the%20availability%20problems)[\[95\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=have%20claimed%20that%20general%20two,layered%20on%20top%20of%20the) (in Spanner’s words, “2PC on top of Paxos” prevents the commit from being lost)[\[96\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=of%20transactions.%20Running%20two,value%20mappings%20supported%20by%20the).

**Fault Tolerance:** With Raft replication, the system can tolerate up to f failures out of 2f+1 replicas for each partition. Committed data remains safe and available as long as a majority of replicas are up. If a follower crashes, the leader continues and the follower catches up from the log when it recovers. If the leader crashes, Raft elects a new leader (this failover typically completes in a few hundred milliseconds after heartbeat timeouts[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20achieves%20consensus%20via%20an,4)[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=either%20a%20leader%20or%20a,4)). To avoid losing recent data on leader crash, we configure the leader to flush log entries to disk before acknowledging clients (synchronous replication). Raft ensures **no split-brain**: it requires a majority, so two different leaders cannot commit conflicting entries concurrently[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20implements%20consensus%20by%20a,servers%20elect%20a%20new%20leader)[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=servers%20without%20consulting%20other%20servers,servers%20elect%20a%20new%20leader).

**Topology:** We often colocate multiple partition groups on the same physical node for efficiency. For example, consider a cluster of 3 nodes with 2 partitions (shards) replicated 3-way. We might assign Node1 as leader for Partition1 and follower for Partition2; Node2 as follower for Partition1 and leader for Partition2; Node3 as follower for both (or leader for a hypothetical Partition3), achieving load-balancing of leadership. **Figure 2** shows an example cluster with two partitions and Raft replication.

![](data:image/png;base64,)  
_Figure 2: High-level cluster architecture (inspired by NebulaGraph_[_\[99\]_](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=Image%3A%20Shared)[_\[100\]_](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=key%2Fvalue%20operations,storage%20hosts%20and%20query%20hosts)_). The graph is partitioned into N shards (Partition 1..N). Each partition is replicated across storage engines on multiple nodes, and a consensus service (Raft) keeps each partition’s replicas consistent. Query engines (compute layer) route operations to the appropriate partition leader. A separate Meta service (right) tracks partition assignment and orchestrates reconfigurations_[_\[101\]_](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=Meta%20Service)[_\[92\]_](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=The%20Storage%20Service%20is%20designed,as%20the%20physical%20data%20storage)_._

**Membership and Reconfiguration:** The **Meta Service** (or configuration manager) keeps track of cluster topology: which nodes host replicas of which partition. When adding a new node, the meta service may instruct some partitions to add a new replica on that node (Raft configuration change) and then possibly remove an old replica to maintain a set size. Raft supports configuration changes by a special joint consensus process to ensure a smooth transition without losing quorum. Similarly, if a node is to be removed, the partitions with replicas on it will replicate to another node first. This meta service itself is a small Raft group (with its own leader) for high availability[\[102\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=Meta%20Service). In NebulaGraph’s architecture, a dedicated Meta RAFT group coordinates such changes[\[102\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=Meta%20Service)[\[103\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=Image%3A%20Meta%20Service). In our design, the meta service stores partition-to-node mappings, and possibly global schema or unique counters (for issuing new vertex IDs, etc.). The meta data is relatively small and changes infrequently, so one Raft group for it (or a few) is sufficient.

**Read Consistency:** By default, clients read from the partition leader to get the latest data (linearizable reads). Raft can also serve **stale reads** from followers if requested (for higher throughput on heavy read workload) – however, followers may lag by a small margin. In many graph scenarios, strong consistency is desired, so we typically route reads to leaders. We do implement Raft’s **lease reads** optimization: after a leader has been elected and it knows no clock drift issues, it can serve reads without an actual round-trip consensus by relying on its leadership lease (ensuring no other leader could have modified data)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Basics)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20achieves%20consensus%20via%20an,4). This is an important performance optimization for read-heavy workloads.

**Geo-Distribution:** While not a primary focus, the design could extend to geo-distributed clusters by placing replicas in different data centers. Raft’s performance would depend on cross-DC latency, but it would still ensure consistency. If global scale is needed, techniques like Google Spanner’s TrueTime-based external consistency[\[105\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=TrueTime%20API%20and%20sketches%20its,of%20and%20rationale%20un%02derlying%20Spanner%E2%80%99s)[\[80\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=directory%20abstraction%2C%20which%20is%20used,development%2Fproduction%20uni%02verse%2C%20and%20a%20production) or Calvin’s deterministic ordering could be explored, but those are beyond our current scope. For now, we assume a cluster in one region with low-latency network (possibly InfiniBand/RDMA as G-Tran uses for speed[\[106\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=InfiniBand%20and%20RDMA,sided%20send%2Frecv%20verbs%20and)[\[107\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=OS,important%20factors%20that%20should%20be)).

## Distributed Transactions and Two-Phase Commit

So far, we’ve covered single-partition operations (a transaction affecting data in one shard). Many graph queries or updates can be confined to a single partition by proper data modeling or by luck of the hash. However, some transactions will inevitably span partitions – e.g., adding an edge between vertices that reside on different shards, or a query that matches a pattern where vertices fall in multiple shards. To maintain ACID **Atomicity** for multi-shard transactions, we implement a classic **Two-Phase Commit (2PC)** protocol[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=In%20transaction%20processing%20%2C%20,To%20accommodate%20recovery%20from)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=1.%20The%20commit,result%20to%20all%20the%20participants) on top of our per-partition transaction managers.

**Two-Phase Commit Overview:** 2PC is an atomic commitment protocol that coordinates all involved partitions (participants) to either commit or abort together[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=the%20two,To%20accommodate%20recovery%20from)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=1.%20The%20commit,result%20to%20all%20the%20participants). We designate one node (typically the partition where the transaction began or the one holding a “coordinator” role) as the **2PC coordinator**. The other involved partitions are **participants**. In the first phase (prepare/vote phase), the coordinator sends a **prepare** message to each participant asking if it can commit[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=1.%20The%20commit,or%20abort). Each participant executes the transaction’s operations on its local data (under 2PL or equivalent) and makes an _internal_ commit decision: if it can commit (all constraints ok, and it has recorded the transaction’s changes in its WAL and is ready to commit), it responds **prepared (Yes)**; if something is wrong (e.g., deadlock, or constraint violation) it responds **No** (meaning it will abort)[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=attempts%20to%20prepare%20all%20the,result%20to%20all%20the%20participants). If any participant votes No, the coordinator will decide to abort the whole transaction. If all vote Yes, the coordinator moves to phase two (completion phase) and sends **commit** messages to all participants[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=abort%20,if%20applicable), otherwise it sends **abort** to those that voted Yes. All participants then follow through (actually commit their local changes on commit message, or roll back if abort)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=abort%20,if%20applicable). This ensures atomicity across shards: either all shards commit their piece or none do. Each participant uses WAL to remember its part of the transaction; importantly, after voting Yes, a participant must **wait for the coordinator’s decision** (this is the blocking nature of 2PC). If the coordinator fails during this window, participants remain in a prepared state (holding locks) until the coordinator recovers or a timeout triggers a recovery procedure.

**Integration with Raft replication:** In our design, each partition’s commit or abort is also subject to Raft replication. The prepare phase involves only the transaction and lock state (not making durable decisions yet except marking an intent in WAL). When the coordinator decides to commit, it will log a commit record for the global transaction (possibly in a separate coordinator log or in one of the participant’s logs designated as coordinator). Running 2PC over Raft/Paxos is a known practice to avoid the window where a coordinator crash can block the system[\[114\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=have%20claimed%20that%20general%20two,with%20per%02formance%20problems%20due%20to)[\[96\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=of%20transactions.%20Running%20two,value%20mappings%20supported%20by%20the). In Spanner’s case, they replicate the commit decision in a Paxos group so that even if the coordinator node fails, the decision is durably stored by the majority and a new coordinator can take over[\[96\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=of%20transactions.%20Running%20two,value%20mappings%20supported%20by%20the). We follow a similar pattern: the **coordinator’s commit decision is stored in a fault-tolerant manner** (either by piggybacking on one of the participant’s Raft logs or a dedicated replicated log). This way, participants can ask the new coordinator (or consult a distributed commit log) to find out the outcome if the original coordinator never responds. Thus we eliminate the need for manual intervention which classic 2PC might require on certain failures[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=specialised%20type%20of%20consensus%20,in%20logging%20strategies%20and%20recovery)[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=communication%2C%20etc,and%20supported%20by%20the%20protocol).

**2PC Message Flow:** To illustrate, consider a transaction adding an edge between Vertex A in Shard1 and Vertex B in Shard2. The client sends the request to Shard1 (coordinator). Shard1’s leader executes the local part (insert half-edge, etc.) and sends prepare to Shard2’s leader. Shard2 does its part and replies prepared. Now coordinator logs a “global commit” (replicated via Raft to ensure durability of decision) and sends commit to Shard2. Both apply changes and release locks, and the transaction commits. **Figure 3** shows a simplified sequence diagram of the 2PC message flow for a successful commit across a coordinator and two participant shards.

![](data:image/png;base64,)  
_Figure 3: Two-Phase Commit sequence across one coordinator and two participant shards. The coordinator issues Prepare() to participants and, on all “prepared” votes, follows with Commit() messages_[_\[111\]_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=1.%20The%20commit,or%20abort)[_\[113\]_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=abort%20,if%20applicable)_. Each participant durably votes (via WAL) and later commits or aborts as instructed, ensuring atomic outcome across shards. In case of any “No” vote or failures, the coordinator would abort the transaction._

**Ensuring Isolation in Distributed Transactions:** We extend our concurrency control to the distributed context by having each partition obey the same locking protocol for the transaction. During the prepare phase, each participant holds all locks for that transaction. If any participant cannot obtain a required lock (meaning a conflict with another transaction), it would either wait (if using 2PL with wait) or roll back (if using deadlock detection or timeout). A _No_ vote may effectively indicate a deadlock or other error, causing a global abort. We must also prevent global deadlocks (cycles where two transactions each hold locks on different shards and wait on the other). A solution is a **global wait-die** scheme or wound-wait that uses global transaction timestamps to break cycles, or a coordinating layer that checks for cross-shard waits. A simpler approach is to use a _global ordering_ of transactions: for instance, assign each distributed transaction a unique timestamp or ID and force a global ordering (this is akin to deterministic CC or using a timestamp CC like Spanner’s TrueTime, but we are sticking to 2PL here). In practice, distributed deadlocks are rare if transactions tend to stay in one shard or access shards in a consistent order.

**Recovery in Distributed Transactions:** If a coordinator crashes after sending prepares, our protocol relies on the replicated log of the coordinator decision. Upon recovery, the coordinator (or a backup) will see in the log if it had decided commit or abort (or see that no decision was logged, implying an abort by default). Participants that are in doubt (prepared and waiting) will contact the coordinator’s shard leader to get the outcome. This is part of the 2PC recovery: all participants log a “prepare received” in their WAL and if they restart in a prepared state, they ping the coordinator for a decision (or possibly the meta service which could store the outcome in a small stable log). Because we integrate with Raft, the window where a coordinator failure causes indefinite blocking is minimized or eliminated: **“Running two-phase commit over Paxos mitigates the availability problems”**[\[94\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=have%20claimed%20that%20general%20two,Paxos%20mitigates%20the%20availability%20problems) as noted in Spanner. We effectively get a fault-tolerant transaction manager.

**Performance considerations:** 2PC introduces additional latency (two network round-trips: prepare and commit) and holds locks longer (until commit messages). For high-throughput scenarios, we implement **transaction batching** and **parallel prepare**: a coordinator can pipeline multiple independent transactions’ prepare/commit messages to reduce overhead. If a multi-shard transaction involves shards 1, 2, 3, the prepare messages to all can be sent in parallel, rather than sequentially. Our commit protocol also supports an optimization if only one shard had data and others are read-only participants: we can **early commit** the others. If distributed transactions are too frequent, one might consider alternative designs like Calvin (deterministic ordering to avoid 2PC) or materializing join tables to avoid cross-shard queries. However, in a graph DB, cross-partition traversals are sometimes unavoidable, so 2PC is the straightforward correctness approach. We ensure that even under 2PC, graph traversals are efficient by localizing as much as possible (e.g., sending subqueries to the shards and aggregating results, rather than shipping all data around).

## Caching and Distributed Query Processing

We briefly touched on caching at the storage layer (buffer pool, object cache). At the cluster level, we also incorporate caching to speed up cross-shard operations. For instance, if a vertex on Shard1 has many edges to vertices on Shard2, and these are traversed frequently, Shard1 may cache some information about the remote vertices (like their properties or a short summary) to avoid repeatedly fetching them. This is analogous to a distributed cache or even replication of read-mostly data. Our design allows configuring certain data as **cached copies** on other shards – but these copies are treated as read-only and invalidated or updated on writes. We utilize a publish/subscribe mechanism via the meta service or Raft to notify other shards if a cached entity is updated, so they can invalidate it. Such caching is kept transparent to users and doesn’t violate consistency because any stale cache is either not used for transactions requiring absolute up-to-date data or is coordinated. An example from research is **distributed snapshot caching**: one could keep a snapshot of the graph for OLAP queries while OLTP continues on the live graph, but that’s outside our OLTP focus.

**Query Engine Considerations:** While not focusing on GQL, note that a distributed query (like a multi-hop traversal that spans shards) is executed through a coordination of subqueries. A query planner will break the query into parts that run on each shard (likely collocated with the storage on that shard for locality) and use a scatter-gather or iterative expansion approach. For example, a BFS traversal starting at a vertex on Shard1 will retrieve neighbors (some on Shard1, some on Shard2…), then it will query Shard2 for those neighbors, and so on. We use an asynchronous, pipelined execution engine where possible: intermediate results (vertex IDs to explore next) are passed to the relevant shard’s query service. Each server’s **query service** is stateless and can execute on a given partition’s data[\[117\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=Stateless%20Query%20Layer), then return results to the coordinator. The coordinator assembles the final results. We employ techniques like **vertex ID bloom filters** to avoid revisiting nodes, etc., to reduce network traffic on graph algorithms. These are beyond ACID, but important for performance.

## Distributed Coordination and Meta-Services

**Metadata Management:** A centralized (replicated) **Metadata Service** keeps track of global metadata: cluster membership, partition assignments, schema definitions (property keys, data types, index configurations), and so on. This service runs as a small replicated database itself (we can use our own engine or an external one). In our implementation, the meta store is a lightweight Raft-backed key-value store (similar to etcd or Zookeeper in functionality). It stores, for example, a mapping of Partition -> \[list of replica nodes, current leader\], and a mapping of Vertex Label -> partitioning strategy (for vertex-cut labels, etc.). The Query engines and storage nodes consult the meta service to route requests correctly. On any configuration change (node add/remove, leader change, partition split), the meta store is updated, and the clients/shards get notifications (or pull updates).

**Distributed Locking and Coordination:** Some operations might need cluster-wide coordination – for instance, creating a new index or performing a global schema change. These are done via **distributed locks** or epoch-based coordination. We provide a mechanism where a special transaction can acquire a lock in the meta service (which effectively uses consensus to agree on one lock holder) before proceeding with a schema update, to ensure no conflicting updates happen. This is similar to how many systems use Zookeeper to coordinate such metadata operations. Our meta service can provide this functionality (with a compare-and-swap on a well-known key implementing a mutex).

For **epoch-based coordination**, we tag each transaction or operation with a global epoch or timestamp (Lamport clock or TrueTime if available) to impose an order. For instance, to take a consistent snapshot across shards, we might use an epoch barrier where all new transactions beyond a point wait until the snapshot is taken.

**Failure handling:** When a node fails, the meta service and Raft groups detect it (missed heartbeats). If the node hosted any leaders, Raft will elect new leaders on other replicas. The meta service can update a list of active nodes and possibly trigger re-replication if a node is down for long (to restore replication factor). Because each shard still functions with a majority, the system continues serving. If an entire shard’s majority is down (which means >f failures in that group), that partition becomes unavailable – but other partitions still work (like partial outage). We strive to design the partitioning such that critical portions of the graph are replicated across independent failure domains to avoid correlated failures taking down a whole partition.

**Consistency Levels:** By default we ensure _strong consistency_ (serializable ACID transactions). However, some use cases might accept lower isolation or consistency for better performance. We could allow read-only transactions to specify a **snapshot isolation** timestamp (then they can read from followers perhaps or a consistent snapshot without locking). We could also allow _optimistic local transactions_ that commit without global atomicity if the user explicitly wants to trade that (similar to eventual consistency in some NoSQL). But these are optional relaxations; our baseline is full ACID across the distributed system.

**Monitoring and Ops:** We include tracing of transactions across shards for debugging (to pinpoint if a transaction is stuck waiting on a lock in another shard, etc.). Each operation can be logged with a trace ID. The meta service might also serve as an aggregate logger for cluster events.

Finally, we emphasize that all these distributed mechanisms have been carefully chosen based on proven approaches in research and industry: _Raft_ for replication[\[118\]](https://www.nebula-graph.io/posts/nebula-graph-architecture-overview#:~:text=stores%20as%20the%20physical%20data,storage) (giving strong consistency and simplicity), _two-phase commit_ for distributed atomicity[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-phase_commit_protocol#:~:text=In%20transaction%20processing%20%2C%20,To%20accommodate%20recovery%20from), and _graph-specific partitioning_ to handle the unique structure of graph data[\[69\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=cuts%20are%20needed%20to%20address,issue%20on%20very%20large%20graphs)[\[66\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Cutting%20a%20vertex%20means%20storing,and%20removing%20the%20hot%20spot). By grounding our design in these principles, we achieve a system that is both **robust in theory and practical in implementation**.

## Conclusion and Trade-off Analysis

In this report, we presented the architecture of a distributed property graph database from the ground up, focusing on the low-level systems engineering required for **ACID transactions** at scale. We covered the storage engine’s slotted-page layout and how it stores graph primitives, drawing from decades of database research for performance and correctness[\[1\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=Slotted%20pages%20work%20by%20splitting,many%20big%20databases%2C%20like%20PostgreSQL)[\[2\]](https://siemens.blog/posts/database-page-layout/#:~:text=The%20header%20region%20stores%20metadata,compression%2C%20sibling%20page%20ids%2C%20etc). We discussed concurrency control choices (2PL for strict serializability)[\[16\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=databases%20to%20implement%20different%20isolation,the%20same%20time%20by%20main%02taining) and the WAL/ARIES protocol for recovery[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=Three%20main%20principles%20lie%20behind,ARIES)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_Recovery_and_Isolation_Exploiting_Semantics#:~:text=The%20recovery%20works%20in%20three,database%20in%20a%20consistent%20state) that ensures durability and atomicity even in the face of failures. Our encryption-at-rest approach and optional enclave support bring state-of-the-art security practices into the design[\[47\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=the%20database%20runs%20in%20an,appends%20and%20truncation%2C%20and%20requires)[\[119\]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/enclavedb.pdf#:~:text=to%20use%20trusted%20execution%20environments,Furthermore%2C%20ensuring%20high).
