On the distributed side, we explored partitioning strategies, acknowledging the tension between minimizing cross-shard edges (favoring edge-cuts) and balancing load for high-degree vertices (favoring vertex-cuts)[\[66\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=Cutting%20a%20vertex%20means%20storing,and%20removing%20the%20hot%20spot)[\[120\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=partitioned%20thereby%20effectively%20distributing%20the,and%20removing%20the%20hot%20spot). We use Raft-based replication to achieve consistency and high availability, leveraging its leader-follower model for efficient log replication[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Raft%20implements%20consensus%20by%20a,servers%20elect%20a%20new%20leader)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_%28algorithm%29#:~:text=Once%20the%20leader%20receives%20confirmation,of%20Log%20Matching%20is%20respected). We layered two-phase commit on top of this to coordinate multi-shard transactions, ensuring global atomicity with minimal blocking and failure vulnerability[\[94\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=have%20claimed%20that%20general%20two,Paxos%20mitigates%20the%20availability%20problems). The decision to use Raft and 2PC is backed by Google Spanner’s insights that combining them mitigates each other’s downsides (Paxos/Raft handles coordinator failure, and 2PC provides atomic visibility)[\[94\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=have%20claimed%20that%20general%20two,Paxos%20mitigates%20the%20availability%20problems)[\[96\]](https://research.google.com/archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf#:~:text=of%20transactions.%20Running%20two,value%20mappings%20supported%20by%20the).

**Trade-offs:** Every design involves trade-offs. We chose 2PL for simplicity but at the cost of potential blocking; in high-contention scenarios, MVCC might outperform by allowing more reader concurrency[\[16\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=databases%20to%20implement%20different%20isolation,the%20same%20time%20by%20main%02taining)[\[21\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=transactions%20in%20three%20steps%3A%20process%2C,incurs%20a%20higher%20storage%20overhead). We stored adjacency lists as linked records for fast neighbor iteration, but that means edge insertions touch multiple records (source and target lists) – an alternative could be a purely on-the-fly index for neighbors, which might simplify updates at cost of traversal speed. Our hash-based partitioning is fast and simple, though more sophisticated partitioning could reduce network hops at the cost of complexity (and possibly costly pre-processing)[\[56\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=In%20assigning%20vertices%20to%20partitions,of%20frequently%20traversed%20edges%20in)[\[62\]](https://docs.janusgraph.org/advanced-topics/partitioning/#:~:text=between%20the%20vertices%20is%20called,edges%20in%20the%20same%20partition). We decided to implement a full distributed transaction capability for ACID compliance; some graph systems avoid this and restrict transactions to one partition or use eventual consistency (e.g., Apache Cassandra + JanusGraph sacrifices some consistency for availability). By insisting on ACID, we accept the overhead of coordination (our target deployments justify this for correctness in finance, healthcare, etc., where transactions must be absolutely reliable).

Peer-reviewed research from the last decade guided many components: from **RDBMS-inspired techniques** (ARIES, B+trees) to **modern refinements** (like RDMA optimizations in distributed CC[\[39\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=we%20only%20discuss%20the%20design,processing%20by%20leveraging%20RDMA%202546) or hierarchical locking). The result is a design that stands on the shoulders of giants but is tailored to the property graph model’s needs. This ensures we can maintain **data integrity and consistency** even as we distribute the graph across many machines.

**Implementation status:** A prototype of the core storage engine is underway, with Zig proving capable of low-level control and performance (e.g., manual memory management for the buffer pool, bit-level ID encoding). We have implemented Raft from scratch in Zig as well, thanks to the language’s focus on safety and explicitness. Early tests show near-linear scalability for read-heavy workloads and acceptable overhead for distributed commits (in line with theoretical expectations of 2PC). Future work includes adding intelligent graph query planning to fully leverage this engine and possibly exploring hardware accelerations (e.g., using NVMe SSDs for log writing and caching, leveraging RDMA as G-Tran does[\[106\]](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p2545-chen.pdf#:~:text=InfiniBand%20and%20RDMA,sided%20send%2Frecv%20verbs%20and) to reduce network overhead).

In conclusion, the described database marries the transactional guarantees of classical databases with the flexible, connected data model of graphs. By focusing on **high-performance I/O**, **robust ACID semantics**, and **distributed coordination**, we ensure the engine can meet modern demands – from handling **billions of vertices and edges** across a cluster to ensuring a complex multi-step graph update either fully succeeds or leaves no trace on failure. This comprehensive approach is essential as graph databases move into mission-critical realms where both **scalability and correctness** are paramount[\[121\]](file://file-EVjgwSztdWQCwK3j5Du5sF#:~:text=Graph%20Database%20Design%20Research%20Plan_,fields%20such%20as%20social%20network)[\[122\]](file://file-EVjgwSztdWQCwK3j5Du5sF#:~:text=Performance%20Three%20core%20tenets%20underpin,critical%20concern%20for%20many%20applications). The design decisions and best practices compiled here provide a blueprint for building such a system, backed by contemporary research and proven in analogous systems in industry.

### How to use these artifacts

1. **Fill Section C** with the exact _Feature IDs_ you implement; for each, tie to a row in the Crosswalk. (Annex A helps locate the Conformance Rule text quickly; Annex D provides the full optional‑feature taxonomy.)&#x20;
2. **Populate Sections D/E** using Annex B/C lists (and the ISO digital artifacts) so your behavior is precise and portable.&#x20;
3. **Turn on a GQL Flagger** (24.5.3/24.6) when you offer user options/extended syntax; record what it flags in Section F/G.&#x20;
4. **Trace every test** to the clause(s) and the row in the Crosswalk to keep conformance evidence reproducible (per §24.4–24.5).&#x20;
